title: Enhanced central chemoreception contributes to breathing problems in hypertension
text:
Hypertension is a is a leading cause of death, and evidence suggests that disordered breathing (commonly
associated with hypertension) contributes to development and maintenance of high blood pressure. Here, I will
determine how respiratory neurons are disrupted in a spontaneously hypertensive rat (SHR) model of
hypertension, and I will test whether treatments that improve respiratory function also improve blood pressure in
this model. I expect results of this work to yield novel insight regarding therapeutic targets for treatment of
cardiorespiratory function in hypertension.

title: Identification of Young Infants with Bronchiolitis at Low Risk of Developing Respiratory Progression
text:
Up to one-third of young infants aged ≤90 days old who present to the emergency department (ED) with viral
bronchiolitis have potentially avoidable hospitalizations, contributing to preventable exposure to hospital-
acquired infections, undue caregiver distress, and high healthcare costs. An accurate clinical prediction model
is needed to identify young infants at low risk of developing respiratory progression who can be safely
discharged to home. Using clinical history and physical examination factors, identification of the etiologic
viruses, and physiologic time series data measured from bedside monitors, the proposed study will create new
prediction models to guide clinical decisions and improve clinical outcomes for young infants with bronchiolitis.

title: Accelerating malaria prevention through enhanced analysis of transmission and RTS,S vaccination in Malawi
text:
Malaria parasite infections and disease continue to cause considerable morbidity and mortality
in Malawi. This research will ascertain why some existing malaria control practices have
become less effective in reducing contact with the mosquito vector and in decreasing the
incidence of malaria disease. A new anti-malaria vaccine for children and bed nets with new
compounds will be evaluated for their ability to reduce disease risk.

title: Fusion pore structure and dynamics
text:
Membrane fusion is a crucial cellular function that mediates key processes including fertilization, viral entry into
host cells, and communication between cells. By focusing on the membrane fusion step that mediates the
release of neurotransmitters, we will gain insights into synaptic transmission, and membrane fusion reactions
in general. These insights will provide novel targets for intervention in mental disorders where exocytosis and
neuronal communication are impaired.

title: Advanced Voltage Indicators Tailored for Two-Photon Resonant Scanning Applications
text:
Genetically encoded voltage indicators (GEVIs) are cutting-edge biosensors that allow scientists to non-invasively monitor
electrical activity in living tissues, enabling the study of brain function, from normal cognitive processes to the mechanisms
underlying neurological disorders. This project seeks to develop next-generation GEVIs specifically optimized for widely
accessible resonant scanning two-photon microscopes, making these powerful tools more practical for researchers
worldwide. By combining advanced biosensor engineering, enhancements to automated screening technologies, and
innovative methods for precisely targeting indicators to brain cells, the team aims to expand the use of GEVIs and unlock
new possibilities for brain research.

title: Macrophage Derived Small Extracellular Vesicles to Resolve Spinal Cord Injury Induced Pain
text:
Small extracellular vesicles (sEV) are nanoparticles that contribute to intercellular communications, and sEV
focused therapies may provide analgesia in preclinical models of chronic pain. Conclusions made from this
study will provide indispensable insight into how sEVs contribute to homeostatic and pathological regulation of
chronic pain after spinal cord injury, aiding efforts to address the desperate need for more effective therapies.

title: Impact of Spatial and Social Determinants on Invasive Fungal Infection Risk
text:
:
Invasive fungal infections (IFIs) are a major public health concern, affecting 13 million people worldwide each year and leading to over 1.5 million deaths. Local contextual factors thought to be crucial risk factors for IFIs, particularly for molds and endemic fungi, but our ability to identify individuals at risk for or infected with IFIs is limited by our incomplete understanding of how specific spatial factors influence the distribution and spectrum of disease. This proposal is designed to elucidate the impact of spatial and social determinants on IFI risk and outcomes to improve prediction of and clinical care for IFIs.

title: Core 2: Genomics
text:
The Genomics Core will assist all four projects, by performing genomics and bioinformatics analyses for this
program project. Genomic data generated by this Core will be used to advance our understanding of the role of
BRCA network in genome maintenance and cancer.

title: Smart nanoparticles regulating oncogenic IncRNA for breast cancer therapy
text:
This project is aimed at developing safe and effective smart lipid siRNA
nanoparticles to regulate long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) associated with cancer
metastasis and drug-resistance in triple-negative breast cancer patients. Tumor-
specific silencing of cancer-promoting lncRNAs with the nanoparticles offers a novel
therapy to treat invasive breast cancer with minimal side-effects, to enhance the
efficacy of chemotherapy and/or immunotherapy, and to eventually eradicate the
disease and improve the survival of cancer patients.

title: Rules of Genome Evolution and Design in Small, Single-Stranded DNA Phages
text:
Microviruses are small bacteriophages that are incredibly abundant in the human gut and elsewhere, and that
have been associated with health conditions such as IBS, Crohn’s Disease, obesity and even cognitive
dysfunction. Since they have eluded standard cultivation methods, we are developing a reverse genetic system
to sample and manipulate these phages. Our research will overcome critical challenges in their cultivation,
determine how these small phages successfully compete with much larger & complex viruses, and pave the
way for biotechnological applications of their versatile genomes.

title: Role of clonal somatic mutations in microglia and Alzheimer’s disease
text:
Alzheimer’s disease (AD) and other neurodegenerative diseases are characterized by age-associated
neuronal loss, which involves neuroinflammation induced by reactive microglia. Our preliminary analyses from
three AD cohorts and with three sequencing technologies consistently revealed an excess of clonal somatic
mutations in AD brains, particularly in proliferation-related genes of microglia. We plan to test our hypothesis
that the accumulation of somatic mutation contributes to an age-related increase in AD risk by driving the
clonal expansion of microglia, which subsequently induces neuroinflammation and neuronal loss in AD brains.

title: The Virginia Advancing Cancer Control Engaged Research through Transformative Solutions Center
text: The VA-ACCERT Center will support four Community Responsive Research Projects across the five-year project period aligned with the goal of improving dissemination and implementation of multi-level cancer health promotion and prevention services to individuals and families living within Virginia’s Department of Housing and Urban Development-administered income-based housing – communities vastly comprised of populations with extremely low socioeconomic status and poor health outcomes. Each project will be led by an academic-community Co-Lead team and will promote iterative, rapid-cycle research that is responsive to the needs of the Center’s partnering income-based housing communities. In addition, these projects will fuel the Center’s efforts to promote the development of early-career investigators focused on multi-level cancer prevention and control and community-engaged research. Ideally, each academic Co-Lead for the four projects will need to meet the NIH definition of an early-stage investigator and include a senior Center-associated mentor; priority will also be given to projects incorporating pre- and postdoctoral trainees. Only Project 1 has been fully developed and described. Projects 2-4 will be selected through an academic-community-led, peer-review process and will receive design, implementation, evaluation, and dissemination support from the Research Methods, Measures, and Data Management Core. Project 1 Summary: Colorectal cancer (CRC) remains the second leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States. Social drivers of health are often associated with screening uptake. Certain groups, such as individuals in income-based housing, are less likely to seek and obtain CRC screening. Project 1 aims to develop a multi-level and peer-led Colon Health Champion intervention, leveraging interpersonal communication and community cohesion, to improve CRC screening awareness and uptake within public housing communities. Utilizing an ORBIT model for behavioral treatment development, Aim 1 will use qualitative methods to collect formative data to identify critical intervention components via key informant interviews and focus groups with CRC screening age-eligible adults living in public housing communities. The Project 1 team will iterate and modify intervention components based on focus group feedback and then identify and train Colon Health Champions to deliver the intervention. In Aim 2, a randomized controlled trial with income-based housing residents will determine the feasibility and preliminary efficacy of the Colon Health Champion intervention, including the impact on screening completion. Collectively, the proposed research will produce a multi-level, peer-led intervention designed to improve CRC health literacy and screening uptake and advance health among residents in income-based housing.

title: High throughput isotropic resolution fluorescence and second Harmonic imaging to characterize tendon injury
text:
This proposal will combine tissue clearing, two photon microscopy, and multiview imaging to develop new and
quantitative tools for investigating animal models of musculoskeletal injuries. These tools will then be applied to
3D spatially map inflammatory cellular and molecular signaling in tendon injury models, leading to a better
understanding of the pathology, which could lead to new therapies.

title: Exploring mechanical mechanisms of antibiotic resistance
text:
Many of our front-line, broad-spectrum antibiotics target the synthesis of the bacterial cell envelope
and ultimately cause cell death via fracture of this structural exoskeleton. Therefore, determining the
molecular basis for the mechanical properties of the cell envelope and, in turn, the mechanisms by
which bacteria modify these properties to promote antibiotic resistance will provide brand new
strategies to combat this crisis based on undermining the mechanical integrity of bacterial cells.
Furthermore, the ability to manipulate the mechanical properties of the cell envelope will provide new
tools with which to probe the mechanics of other important physiological processes important for
pathogenesis, such rapid proliferation and adaptation to environmental fluctuations.

title: Enhancing precision medicine for brain metastases using interpretable and integrative deep learning
text:
While checkpoint inhibitors (ICI) have emerged as a promising therapy for brain metastases (BM) of diverse
histologies, an unmet need is the lack of a predictive biomarker for ICI efficacy given the high toxicity rate of ICI.
Therefore, the goal of this proposal is to apply deep learning to integrate widely available data modalities in brain
MRI, histopathology, and clinico-genomic data for BM patients treated with ICI. Our work should result in an
improved predictive biomarker for ICI efficacy and provide a strategic framework by which to integrate clinically
relevant data modalities to study therapeutic efficacy in other tumor types.

title: Exploiting the Metabolic Dependencies of Pediatric AML
text:
A common type of childhood cancer, acute myelogenous leukemia (AML), affects approximately
500 U.S. children annually, and only about half survive. This project will examine how to target
the metabolic dependencies of pediatric AML. Additionally, we will test a well-tolerated drug for
incorporation into treatment for pediatric AML.

title: Hormonal Regulation of HSV-1 Replication in Neurons
text:
In our laboratory, we found that herpes virus infection in neuronal cells was controlled in part by thyroid
hormone. This discovery may be critical in understanding viral reactivation. We propose specific
experiments to investigate the detailed mechanisms using different models, and the results from the studies
will benefit our knowledge and contribute to the development of therapeutic agents.

title: Understanding neural control of the ocular surface
text:
New technologies, methods and models are needed to advance our scientific understanding of how the nervous
system maintains the surface of the eye. We will apply several new technologies, animal models, and methods
to study molecular, cellular, and functional interactions across the surface of the eye and regions controlling it.
We will compare how these interactions change under inflammatory and pain conditions.

title: Tradeoffs between fitness costs and transfer rates in horizontal gene transfer
text:
Horizontal gene transfer is one of the main contributors to the worldwide spread of
antibiotic resistance, with especially high prevalence in diverse and dense microbial
communities, most notably the gut microbiome. This work will provide fundamental,
mechanistic insights into the mechanisms underlying the spread of conjugative plasmids
encoding antibiotic resistance. These insights have implications for predicting and
controlling plasmid fates for medical and biotechnological applications. In particular, this
work will significantly contribute to ongoing efforts to develop strategies of antibiotic
treatments that efficiently eliminate pathogens with minimized risk of drug resistance
spreading.

title: Neurophysiological mechanisms of oxytocinergic signaling in the dentate gyrus
text:
PROJECT NARRATIVE.
While social memory is an essential skill for learning to navigate our world, our knowledge of how the brain
processes social memory is limited. This project aims to identify the neural mechanisms influencing social
memory processing in the dentate gyrus, with a focus on oxytocinergic signaling, and its implications for
neuropsychiatric disorders characterized by social deficits, such as Fragile X syndrome. This research will
improve our understanding of oxytocin’s role in dentate gyrus signaling, and may uncover potential therapeutic
targets for improving social cognition in neuropsychiatric disorders.
